bp: A city trying to become climate-neutral is not just choosing nicer buildings or cleaner buses. It is trying to understand how today's planning choices will keep changing emissions, mobility, housing, services, and liveability over many years. This paper serves that need by focusing on scenario-building: the practice of asking, in a disciplined way, what different futures might follow from current development and planning processes. The ordinary object is a city full of records, maps, sensor feeds, plans, forecasts, public input, and organizational routines. The practical question is whether those pieces can be joined into pictures of possible futures that are good enough to guide climate action. The paper is a position paper, so its central contribution is not a new predictor. It argues that time itself is a major obstacle in data-driven climate transition work, especially when digital twins, GIS, simulation, forecasting, decision-support tools, participatory methods, and city workflows must be connected.
wh: The hard part is that urban climate planning depends on information that ages, arrives late, disappears, or cannot be lined up cleanly with other information. A building dataset may describe one year, a transport dataset another, and a planning process may move on a political timetable that does not match either source. Data quality problems are temporal when the numbers are not only noisy but stale, irregular, or recorded at the wrong moment for the decision being made. Data availability is temporal when a planner needs evidence about future consequences but only has partial traces of the past and present. Integration is temporal when tools update at different rhythms or describe time differently. The result is that a scenario can look precise while quietly mixing incompatible clocks. That is dangerous for climate-neutral cities because the whole purpose is to reason across time: what current development produces later emissions reductions, climate action, and liveability.
naive: A smart beginner might gather every urban dataset available, connect it to a map, run a forecasting or simulation tool, and compare the projected futures. That sounds reasonable because scenario-building appears to be a data volume problem: more data should mean better futures. It fails because the datasets may not describe the same moments, the same boundaries, or the same versions of the city. A digital twin may be current in one district and outdated in another. A GIS layer may use administrative areas that do not match a simulation model. Public participation may capture concerns after a plan has already changed. The naive approach treats time as a label on data, when time is part of the data's meaning.
ap: The core idea is to make temporal challenges visible before trusting the scenario. Instead of treating scenario-building as a final calculation placed on top of city data, the paper treats it as a chain of time-sensitive handoffs. Current development and planning processes create evidence. That evidence moves through systems such as GIS, digital twins, simulations, forecasts, participatory channels, and decision-support tools. Each handoff can lose timing, context, freshness, or compatibility. The paper's central move is therefore diagnostic: ask where data quality, data availability, and integration problems arise because the city, the data, the tools, and the organization are all moving at different speeds. This reframes climate-neutral planning from a question of simply choosing a model to a question of whether the whole data and workflow system can sustain reliable reasoning about possible futures.
mech: The mechanism begins with the planning object: a city trying to reduce emissions, take climate action, and increase liveability. Into the process come descriptions of the current city and its planned changes. Some descriptions are spatial, such as GIS layers; some are operational, such as organizational workflows; some are model-based, such as digital twins, simulations, and forecasting tools; some are social, such as participatory approaches. Scenario-building then asks how current development and planning processes could unfold over time. To do that, each tool must receive inputs whose timing and meaning are clear. The first check is quality: are the records accurate enough for the period they claim to describe? The second check is availability: is the needed evidence present when the decision has to be made, or is the scenario forced to guess? The third check is integration: can one tool's time scale, spatial boundary, and update rhythm be used by another tool without changing the meaning? The output is not a single guaranteed future. It is a set of scenarios whose usefulness depends on the temporal coherence of the pipeline that produced them. If that pipeline mixes old maps, newer forecasts, partial public input, and planning workflows without tracking their timing, the scenario becomes less a guide and more a polished artifact of mismatched evidence.
math: The main mathematical idea is temporal modeling, which means representing change rather than treating the city as a frozen picture. A scenario is a conditional story: if these current plans, constraints, and trends continue or change, then these later outcomes may follow. That requires sequences, because order matters; a transport intervention before a housing shift can mean something different from the same intervention after it. It also requires uncertainty, because city futures cannot be observed directly. Probability is the language for admitting that evidence is partial and that several futures remain possible. Integration adds another mathematical burden: different data sources must be aligned so that their times, places, and meanings can be compared. This is a matching problem, not just a storage problem. A GIS layer, a digital twin state, and a forecasting input all need compatible reference points. Scenario-building also uses optimization in the plain sense of comparing possible choices against goals such as emission reduction, climate action, and liveability. The tradeoff is speed versus trust: cities need timely decision support, but fast scenarios built from stale or misaligned evidence can create false confidence.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's recurring concern with optimization because urban climate transition is a choice problem under constraints: planners compare possible actions by how well they move a city toward lower emissions and better liveability. It also connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work, but at a broader planning level. Many papers forecast traffic, recover movement traces, or model temporal questions; this paper asks what happens when the surrounding urban data system cannot keep time consistently enough for those tools to support policy. It also sits near data integration and decision-support research. The shared deeper problem is that useful decisions require evidence to travel across boundaries without losing meaning. Here the boundaries are between maps, digital twins, simulations, forecasts, participatory processes, and organizational workflows. Unlike a paper that proposes one forecasting method, this position paper emphasizes the infrastructure and assumptions needed before forecasting can responsibly guide climate-neutral city planning.
ww: The approach works as a conceptual move because scenario-building is only as reliable as the time assumptions underneath it. A planner does not merely need numbers about buildings, traffic, or emissions; the planner needs to know when those numbers were observed, what period they stand for, how often they change, and whether another tool is interpreting them in the same way. By naming temporal challenges in data quality, availability, and integration, the paper pushes attention to the points where false certainty enters. This improves on the naive approach because it does not let a technically impressive simulation hide weak inputs. It also fits urban climate work because cities change through interacting processes: construction, policy, mobility, infrastructure, participation, and administration all unfold at different speeds. A scenario that respects those speeds can better show the implications of current development and planning. The gain is not automatic correctness. The gain is a clearer test of whether a proposed scenario deserves trust.
po: The payoff is a practical agenda for climate-neutral city planning: before relying on data-driven scenarios, cities can inspect where time breaks the chain of evidence. They can ask whether their digital twins are current enough, whether GIS layers match the planning period, whether simulations and forecasts can exchange inputs cleanly, whether participatory evidence arrives in time to shape decisions, and whether organizational workflows preserve the timing context. The paper's result is therefore a framing and diagnostic contribution. It helps planning teams see temporal data problems as central to emission reduction, climate action, and liveability work, not as minor technical cleanup after the real planning is done.
limits: The abstract identifies the challenge but does not claim a tested algorithm, benchmark, dataset, or deployed city system. Because it is a position paper, its value depends on whether the temporal categories it highlights are useful to planners and tool builders in real workflows. The argument assumes that better scenario-building can improve climate-transition decisions, but the abstract does not prove which temporal fixes most improve outcomes. It also does not specify how to resolve conflicts between data sources, how to measure scenario trustworthiness, or how participatory and organizational timing should be weighted against technical data timing. The paper should be read as a map of problems to examine, not as evidence that those problems have been solved.
